API Reference Overview

ATOM SDK provides Python, C++, C# three sets of language bindings, and the interface shapes are completely aligned. AtomClient is a unified entrance, exposing 4 Service: GraphService, NodeService, GraphNodeService, RuntimeService.

overall relationship

                               ┌──────────┐
                               │ your program │
                               └──────────┘
                                     │
                              ┌────────────┐
                              │ AtomClient │
                              │ (unified entrance) │
                              └────────────┘
                                     │
        ┌────────────────┬───────────┴───────┬────────────────────┐
        │                │                   │                    │
┌──────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐
│ GraphService │  │ NodeService │  │ GraphNodeService │  │ RuntimeService │
│    whole picture     │  │  Main graph node    │   │   Subgraph internal nodes    │   │   Runtime execution    │
└──────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────┘

GraphService manages the life cycle of the entire graph (create/open/import/export/run/release) and is responsible for timestamp synchronization; NodeService and GraphNodeService edit nodes on this basis (corresponding to the main graph and subgraph respectively), and expose parameters or output ports as stable names through set_binding_name; RuntimeService uses these binding names to load the graph, set parameters, send data and read binding output.

The two most common routes used

Route 1: Create or modify a diagram (edit mode)

This situation belongs to the "editing state", mainly using GraphService, NodeService and GraphNodeService.

client.graph.create_graph()
    ↓
client.graph.open_graph()
    ↓
client.node.create_node()
    ↓
client.node.set_node_param_data()
    ↓
client.node.connect_nodes()
    ↓
client.graph.run_graph()
    ↓
client.graph.release_graph()

If you want to edit a submap inside a graph node, replace the client.node. in the middle with client.graph_node..

Route 2: Run the ready-made graph in the business program (running state)

This situation belongs to the "running state", mainly using RuntimeService.

client.runtime.load_graph()
    ↓
client.runtime.get_meta_info()
    ↓
client.runtime.set_shared_params()
client.runtime.set_run_params()
    ↓
client.runtime.run_graph()
    ↓
client.runtime.get_binded_output_value()
client.runtime.get_binded_point_cloud_parsed()
    ↓
client.runtime.release_graph()

This route is not responsible for building the graph and is more suitable for the production environment: the graph has been configured in Atom, and the external program is only responsible for feeding input and getting output.

The boundaries of each Service

Service Main issues Typical interface Suitable for scenarios

GraphService

How to manage this picture itself?

create_graph、open_graph、run_graph、export_graph

Create, open, import and export, and debug the entire image

NodeService

How to manage the nodes in the main graph?

create_node、connect_nodes、set_node_param_data、get_node_port_data

Add and delete nodes, connections, parameter settings, and read port results

GraphNodeService

How to manage subgraph nodes?

open_graph、create_node、connect_nodes、run_graph

Operation graph node Internal subgraph

RuntimeService

How to run the map that has been set up?

load_graph、set_run_params、run_graph、get_binded_output_value

External system integration, production inference, reading binding output

easily confused relationship

GraphService.run_graph and RuntimeService.run_graph

They have similar names but different uses:

  • GraphService.run_graph: Run the entire graph in editing mode, suitable for debugging, and depends on timestamp.

  • RuntimeService.run_graph: Send normal RuntimeFrame or passive binocular EPICRAW3 in running state, suitable for continuous calling by business systems.

NodeService and GraphNodeService

The interfaces of the two are very similar, the difference is that the operating positions are different:

  • NodeService To operate the nodes in the main graph, only graph_name and node_id are needed.

  • GraphNodeService operates nodes inside graph node, requiring graph_name, graph_node_id and inside node_id.

Relationship between binding name and Runtime

NodeService.set_binding_name or GraphNodeService.set_binding_name will expose a parameter or output port as a stable name. Then RuntimeService can use this name:

  • Set parameters: set_shared_params, set_run_params

  • Reading results: get_binded_output_value, get_binded_point_cloud_parsed

Version and result type differences

  • Python directly returns dict, list, bytes or point cloud analysis results, and exceptions are expressed through the AtomSdkError system.

  • C++ returns atom::sdk::JsonValue type, ByteBuffer or structured point cloud. Complex input uses *Ref, *Params, *Update structures uniformly.

  • The original interface of C# returns JsonElement, the generic overload returns Task<T>, and the common interface additionally provides a strongly typed result model; all requests support CancellationToken.

All three languages ​​follow the same service boundaries, timestamp rules, binding name rules, and RuntimeFrame/passive_bino two run input modes. The only differences are in language type and asynchronous/exception expressions.
